Researchers had thought that these ancient hominins had been limited to savannahs and open woodlands, claims Kira Westaway, a geochronologist and a co-author of two latest studies. “This is a really massive deal, because we thought Homo sapiens were the only species that had the skill set to survive in really challenging rainforest environments.”.

Reference: Nature paper 1 & paper 2.

It has been revealed that artificial-intelligence giant Anthropic has made history with the largest initial public offering (IPO) on record on 19 November. The firm — now valued at a staggering US$1.5 trillion — has major ambitions in science. It made waves earlier this year when it reported that its model Claude had made several major mathematics breakthroughs. The organization also launched their first ‘wet’ laboratory for life sciences research and has declared prepares to “substantially” scale up its work in AI-enabled drug discovery. Pitched as a company that prioritizes AI safety, some researchers question whether an IPO — and the accompanying investor demands — might disrupt some of Anthropic’s safety commitments.

Roughly 180 million people could be carrying a previously unknown type of giant virus in their guts. Researchers found DNA from these ‘egoviruses’ in gut samples from people, buffalo, goats, chickens, deer and pigs. Six clades were unique to people, one of which is estimated to be present in roughly 1% of the population. Microbiologists say that egoviruses could be the missing link between giant viruses that infect single-celled organisms and distantly related poxviruses, such as those that cause smallpox and mpox, which can infect people and animals directly.

Here in Washington DC, tens of thousands of researchers have gathered for the Society for Neuroscience’s annual meeting — a showcase for everything from neural implants to memory research.

According to recent reports, but when I asked a panel of leaders at the US National Institutes of Health what in neuroscience remains underappreciated, several pointed to the brain’s relationship with the rest of the body. Nora Volkow, director of the National Institute on Drug Abuse, lamented the lack of research into brain metabolism — a blind spot exposed by the surprising neurological effects of GLP-1 drugs.

Amy Bany Adams, acting director of the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, offered a reminder of how much remains to be discovered. Of the glymphatic system, the brain’s waste-clearance network, she said: “We didn’t even know it existed when I was in graduate school.” I’m leaving with a longer list of questions about what else we’ve been overlooking.

Neuroscientists are uncovering how the brain orchestrates a tailored mixture of symptoms in response to either a bacterial or viral infection. Presenting at the Society for Neuroscience’s annual meeting on 15 November, researchers suggested that the brain decodes the type of pathogen that has invaded, accesses memories of past bouts of illness and can even mobilize immune defences at the sight of a sick person. The unpublished findings challenge the long-held view that neurological responses to infection are a one-size-fits-all response to inflammation.

In a recent development, artificial-intelligence governance requires more than companies’ oversight of their models — it requires “a system of accountability” that works like a national constitution, argues legal scholar Cindy Skach. Firms should be held legally liable when individuals are affected by AI actions that infringe on their fundamental rights, Skach suggests. She proposes ‘human dignity’ as the most crucial value for the system to uphold. When a person’s dignity is violated — by an AI-generated deepfake or by a chatbot that treats a distressed user as just another interaction — they could petition a court directly to hold the perpetrator accountable.

Do you find networking a nightmare? Three experts share — in the form of short videos — how to grasp the nettle. They suggest thinking about networking as a professional skill that can be learnt and developed, considering arriving early for events and not worrying about volume. One high-quality connection and follow-up conversation is worth more than 100 business cards, says public-speaking coach Susie Ashfield.

In the second episode of Nature Podcast’s climate miniseries, host Nick Petrić Howe hears from scientists about what humanity can actually do to stop the runaway train of rising temperatures. The rise of renewable-energy technologies is already making a dent in greenhouse-gas emissions, experts say. But creating meat alternatives and a move away from an economic system that incentivizes ‘growth at any cost’ could help to really shift the dial.

Nature Podcast | 45 min listen or read the transcript.

According to recent reports, vertebrate palaeontologist Aldo Benites-Palomino explains why the extinct ancient whale — which evolved extreme facial asymmetry to to make space in its head for echolocation and sound production organs — was named with a Peruvian word for “anything that is flashy, over-the-top, bizarre, extravagant or difficult to categorize aesthetically”. (Discover | 7 min read).

Reference: Communications Biology paper.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03797-3.

Recent findings suggest that today I’m considering buying a prickly pear cactus (Opuntia) in case of a power cut. Researchers have found that the plants’ unusual method of photosynthesis can be harnessed to generate a small amount of electricity, with around eight prickly pears together generating nearly three times the voltage of a standard AA battery.

Your feedback on this newsletter gives me all the charge I need. Please send your thoughts to briefing@nature.com.

Jacob Smith, associate editor, Nature Briefing.

The complete Chelsea hierarchy retain full faith in Xabi Alonso and trust the 44-year-old implicitly, according to Italian transfer guru Fabrizio Romano.

While there might have been a huge amount of excitement around west London following Alonso’s blockbuster arrival at Stamford Bridge over the summer, Chelsea suddenly find themselves at the heart of another public crisis.

Marking their return from November’s international break with a nightmare 4-1 drumming at home against historic rivals Leeds on Saturday, the Stamford Bridge support have made their frustrations abundantly clear.

Tumbling down the Premier League standings, Chelsea have now lost four of their previous five appearances across all competitions on either side of November’s fortnight interval.

Opening the 2026/27 campaign with their sole focus set on booking an essential Champions League return, pressure has started to mount on Alonso’s shoulders in west London.

However, Romano suggested on Monday that both the Chelsea ownership and football leadership team maintain full faith in the former Real Madrid boss and their focus is now on fixing their glaring defensive problems.

Hit for four against Leeds at Stamford Bridge over the weekend, Chelsea have already shipped 20 Premier League goals so far this season and the Blues have mustered just a pair of clean sheets from any of their 13 appearances against top-flight opposition across all competitions.

Alonso officially put pen to paper on a four-year deal in SW6 back in May and remarkably became the third permanent manager in west London in the space of a calendar year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitaly Janelt scored a 30-yard screamer as Brentford romped to a 4-0 victory against 10-man Everton at the Gtech Community Stadium.

One win in five had seen some of the early season optimism around Keith Andrews’ team fade but this was an emphatic response to fire them up the Premier League table to sixth, even if culpability for Everton’s collapse lay largely with James Tarkowski, red carded in the 40th minute for a horror tackle on Yehor Yarmolyuk.

David Moyes was setting a fresh record for number of games in charge, this his 593rd match eclipsing the tally of Harry Catterick racked up during the 60s and 70s, but this was a terrible first half and was no way to mark such an achievement.

Everything went wrong for the visitors. Both Brentford goals scored by Keane Lewis-Potter came via deflections and Tarkowski’s momentary abdication of responsibility as captain, lunging studs-up into the shin of Yarmolyuk with his team 2-0 down, would have been impossible for Moyes to mitigate. He was let down badly by one of his senior players in a moment of direst need.

Recent findings suggest that thereafter the game was little contest. It might have trickled towards a routine two-goal win for Brentford had Janelt not pulled out a brilliant strike from range that ripped past Jordan Pickford to rub salt in the wound for Moyes, and for Tarkowski.

Fabio Carvalho bundled one in from on the goal-line with his knee in stoppage time, the final indignity for Everton.

In a recent development, brentford were excellent throughout. Early on, Callum Wilson fed Michael Kayode arriving up on the right, the full-back given a clear shot on Pickford’s goal but dragged his effort badly across the face and wide.

Everton were making it too easy. Midway through the half they failed to deal with a ball over the top and Jaidon Anthony sent it low into the middle with a deft stab of the toe. It was a beautifully controlled first-time pass, finding Lewis-Potter arriving in an acre of space and his shot spun in off the lunging Jarrad Branthwaite.

It took less than two minutes for Lewis-Potter to hit a near-identical second, with a ball into the box from Mikkel Damsgaard met with unconvincing Everton defending.

The Brentford midfielder was given two attempts, his first shot rebounding back to him to squeeze the ball in at the second go via a deflection off Thierno Barry.

It has been revealed that everton were sinking and their captain abandoned them to their fate. Tarkowski was first shown only a yellow for a studs-up challenge on Yarmolyuk. A single look at a replay confirmed the foul was far more serious, the defender’s boot connecting high on the shin of Yarmolyuk’s standing leg and his dismissal was inevitable.

Jack Grealish came on to try to raise the visitors’ level in his first appearance after five games absent for disciplinary matters.

It made no difference. When Janelt’s 30-yard rocket flew past Pickford midway through the second half it was the cue for some away supporters to begin the long journey home, and few of them witnessed Carvalho’s stoppage-time tap-in. It had been a chastening night for all connected with their club.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andoni Iraola still has several positions among his ranks that he needs to upgrade.

This summer, the Spaniard and Richard Hughes spent around £150 million trying to bolster the Reds' ranks as much as they could.

Obviously, this didn't work out how they'd have wanted it to with some fans left questioning whether the moves that they've made were worthwhile or not.

Some players have more than made their mark but others have failed.

The ones who failed are likely to be replaced with Milos Kerkez now one of the many players on Iraola's chopping block.

Daniel Svensson is coming to take Milos Kerkez's role.

Left-back has been a sore spot for Liverpool recently.

The Anfield outfit have failed to have one of their players put in a decent performance at left-back with fans demanding that a upcoming signing is made.

Alejandro Balde is the most likely candidate at the moment with some murmurings of Lewis Hall also being considered by Liverpool.

At the moment, Kerkez is sharing the responsibility with Kostas Tsimikas and, even though the Greek scouser is supposed to be the more experienced player of the two, he's somehow performed even worse than the Hungarian.

Each time Kerkez or Tsimikas features for the Reds, fans demand that the other is brought on due to how poorly they've been performing.

That's why these recent links with Daniel Svensson are something that the Reds' fans should take seriously.

"According to information from fussball-news.de, Liverpool and Arsenal from the Premier League are showing the greatest interest, while Manchester United and Leeds United are also keeping a close eye on the player," they wrote.

"It is mentioned that the scouting team of the 'Red Devils' observed him in the Champions League game against Real Betis and produced a report with the rating 'transferable/signable'".

"According to information from fussball-news.de, the management of Borussia Dortmund is still committed to keeping Svensson – who has a long-term contract running until June 2029 – and does not want to let him leave.

Industry observers note that "Whether the club completely closes its doors depends on the conditions put on the table. While the club doesn't consider the player untouchable, it is reluctant to let him go unless suitable conditions are met and prepares to strengthen its commitment through a salary increase.

"Borussia Dortmund are hoping for at least €45 million if a sale goes through. Should competition intensify, the total package, including add-ons, could potentially reach €50 million, with performance-related bonuses and sell-on clauses likely to be decisive factors in any deal.

"Premier League clubs are reportedly prepared to test his situation with a €30 million offer for the Swedish player. However, the player is said to be happy in Dortmund and not planning a hasty move.".

Milos Kerkez needs to get back to his best soon.

Kerkez may have been in "brilliant" form for Hungary recently but, that has not been replicated at Anfield.

Every time he features, it feels like he makes a mistake that ends up costing Liverpool the game.

Whether it's a misplaced pass, a mis-timed tackle or even something just as simple as a poor clearance, he's always doing something to mess things up for the Anfield outfit.

That's why, even though he may feel untouchable in his current role, he needs to step things back up.

If he doesn't manage to do this, it's clear that he's going to be finished at Anfield.

Indeed, he's still only 23 years old so there's still a lot of his career left to go but, right now, it doesn't really feel like his future is all that bright, despite the £40 million fee that Liverpool paid for him last summer.
